meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There are no solutions. There are only trade-offs'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Thomas Sowell: the line is in The Vision of the Anointed (1995), not in A Conflict of Visions, the book quote sites usually cite.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: b. 1930 · American economist, senior fellow at the Hoover Institution
answer.sourceLine: Sowell wrote it in The Vision of the Anointed: Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy (BasicBooks, 1995). The book prints it as one sentence with a semicolon: “There are no solutions; there are only trade-offs.” The popular two-sentence version only changes the punctuation. It does not come from A Conflict of Visions, the book quote sites usually name.

trail: We searched inside books with Open Library and found the exact semicolon sentence in Sowell’s The Vision of the Anointed. The same search shows later books repeating it: Open Library search inside ↗
The Internet Archive catalog record ↗ confirms the edition we searched: The vision of the anointed, Sowell, Thomas, 1930–, New York: BasicBooks, 1995.
A full-text search of the same scan finds the line three times: once on its own and twice as variations (“no ‘solutions’ in the tragic vision, but only trade-offs”). IA full-text results ↗

Goodreads lists the source as A Conflict of Visions. A full-text search of that book’s 1987 scan turns up a section called “Trade-offs versus solutions,” which makes the same argument in other words: IA full-text results ↗

author.bio: Thomas Sowell, born in Gastonia, North Carolina, in 1930, is an American economist. He is the Rose and Milton Friedman Senior Fellow on Public Policy at the Hoover Institution. His books include A Conflict of Visions (1987), The Vision of the Anointed (1995) and Basic Economics. Across them he keeps returning to one idea: trade-offs rather than solutions.

misattribution.heading: The wrong-book problem
misattribution.intro: The quote really is Sowell’s. What usually goes wrong is the source. Quote sites send readers to the wrong book, and the wording has been tidied up as it spread.

items.why: Goodreads ↗ and similar sites name this book as the source. Its section “Trade-offs versus solutions” makes the same argument, saying the constrained vision “deals in trade-offs rather than solutions” (IA full text ↗). We searched the 1987, 2002 and 2007 scans of the book, and none of them contains the exact sentence.

items.who: “There are no solutions. There are only trade-offs.”
items.why: Sowell’s 1995 book uses a semicolon, not two sentences. Popular books spread the two-sentence form, for example Greg McKeown’s Essentialism: “economist Thomas Sowell wrote: ‘There are no solutions. There are only trade-offs.’” (Open Library search inside ↗). The meaning is the same.

Similar wording appears before Sowell’s 1995 book. George Radwanski’s Trudeau (1978) says “there are no solutions in government these days, only trade-offs between com-peting” (IA full text ↗). So the idea, in roughly these words, was already in use. The crisp sentence people quote today is the one Sowell printed.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Thomas Sowell’s own words, printed in The Vision of the Anointed (BasicBooks, 1995): “There are no solutions; there are only trade-offs.” (IA full text ↗)

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: Sowell built two books around a contrast. One way of seeing the world expects problems to have solutions. The other treats them as trade-offs, where every gain costs something somewhere else. In The Vision of the Anointed he compresses that into one line, and he uses the same idea in Basic Economics, which says “there are no ‘solutions’ but only trade-offs” (2007 edition, IA full text ↗).

The line may also have been spoken before it was printed. Economist Harold Winter, in Trade-offs (University of Chicago Press, 2005), writes that the quote “was made by Thomas Sowell at a talk he gave at Ohio University in 1992” (Open Library search inside ↗). That is Winter’s memory, not a recording, so the 1995 book remains the documented text.
